title: Insulin Plant (Costus igneus): Benefits, Uses, Side Effects and What Science Says
excerpt: Can the insulin plant (Costus igneus) lower blood sugar? What studies, doctors and popular YouTube channels say, how to use it safely, and how to grow it.
content:
Quick answer: The insulin plant (Costus igneus, now classified as Chamaecostus cuspidatus) is a leafy garden plant from Brazil that many Indian families grow for blood sugar. Animal studies show its leaves can lower blood glucose, but it contains no insulin and has no large human trials behind it. It cannot cure diabetes or replace your medicines, and taking it alongside them can push your sugar too low.

If you live in India, there is a good chance someone has handed you a cutting of this plant with the advice to chew a leaf every morning. In Kerala and Tamil Nadu it sits in pots on verandas and balconies. In the US and UK it is mostly sold as an ornamental called fiery costus or spiral flag, and it turns up in health videos promising a natural fix for diabetes. Below I go through what the plant is, what the research actually found, what popular YouTube channels say about it, and how to stay safe if you want to try it.

What is the insulin plant?

The insulin plant is a perennial herb in the family Costaceae, a close relative of the gingers. Most Indian sources still call it Costus igneus, but botanists now list that name as a synonym of Chamaecostus cuspidatus. Its common English names include fiery costus, spiral flag and step ladder.

Despite its reputation as a traditional Indian remedy, the plant is not native to India. Kew's plant checklist places its natural range in eastern Brazil, in the states of Bahia and Espírito Santo. A 2014 review in Pharmacognosy Reviews by Hegde and colleagues describes it as a fairly recent introduction to India from the Americas, brought in as a herbal cure for diabetes, which is how it got the name "insulin plant." So its use for blood sugar in India is a few decades old, not centuries old.

How do you identify the insulin plant?

The easiest giveaway is the leaf arrangement. The leaves wrap around the stem in a slow spiral, like a staircase, which is where the names spiral flag and step ladder come from. Here is what to look for:

FeatureWhat you will see
HeightUsually about 2 feet (around 60 cm); tall stems tend to flop over
LeavesSmooth, oblong, 4 to 8 inches long, dark green on top with a light purple tinge underneath
Leaf arrangementSpiral around an upright, fleshy stem
FlowersOrange, about 1.5 inches across, on cone-like heads at the stem tips in warm months
RootsUnderground rhizomes that form clumps
Accepted nameChamaecostus cuspidatus (synonym Costus igneus)

Nurseries sometimes sell other Costus species under the same "insulin plant" label, including ones with yellow or red striped flowers. If the flowers are not orange, you probably have a different plant, and the research below may not apply to it.

Does the insulin plant actually lower blood sugar?

In animals, yes, fairly consistently. In people, the evidence is thin.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Pharmacognosy Journal pulled together 14 studies published between 2000 and 2025. Across the experimental studies, treatment with the plant lowered fasting blood glucose by about 31 mg/dL compared with untreated diabetic controls. The authors still concluded that clinical studies are needed before anyone can call it a therapy.

A few individual studies give a sense of what that research looks like:

  • In a 2008 study in the Indian Journal of Experimental Biology, powdered leaves fed to diabetic rats at 500 mg per kg of body weight lowered blood glucose by about 21% after 15 days.
  • A 2010 study in the International Journal of Ayurveda Research gave rats with steroid-induced high blood sugar 100 to 500 mg per kg of powdered leaf per day and compared it with the diabetes drug glibenclamide.
  • A 2013 lab study isolated an "insulin-like protein" from the leaves that lowered blood glucose in mice when given by mouth. It was structurally different from human insulin.

The human data is much smaller. The Hegde review mentions one cross-sectional study in which people with diabetes ate one fresh leaf or one teaspoon of shade-dried leaf powder a day along with their regular treatment and had better blood sugar control. That design cannot show whether the leaf caused the improvement. As of January 2026, Dr. Hari Kishan Boorugu, a diabetologist at Yashoda Hospitals in Hyderabad, told Medical Dialogues there were "no randomised controlled trials" and that doctors cannot recommend it for clinical use yet.

Does the insulin plant contain insulin?

No. The name comes from what people hoped it would do, not from what is inside it. Insulin is a protein hormone, and your stomach breaks proteins down, so even a leaf full of insulin would not work like an injection. The leaves do contain plant compounds that researchers think may affect blood sugar, including triterpenoids such as corosolic acid and lupeol, along with flavonoids, saponins, alkaloids, tannins, steroids and phenolic compounds. Early screening also found protein, iron, vitamin C, vitamin E and beta-carotene in the leaves.

What do popular YouTube channels say about the insulin plant?

Search "insulin plant" on YouTube and you get thousands of videos in English, Hindi, Tamil, Odia and Tagalog. Many promise that chewing two or three leaves a day will "normalize" your sugar. A few well-known channels are more careful, and they are worth hearing out.

SugarMD, a large diabetes channel run by an endocrinologist, says the evidence is mixed: some viewers report that the plant helped and others noticed nothing. The video calls claims that every patient improved or cut their insulin dose in half "partially true" at best, and warns that the biggest risk is a dangerous drop in blood sugar, especially with unknown doses from unfamiliar supplement makers. It also mentions stomach upset, diarrhea and dizziness as possible side effects. The channel sells its own supplements and pitches them in the same video, so treat its comparisons with that in mind.

Plant Abundance, a US gardening channel, plants the insulin plant from rhizomes in a backyard food forest. The host notes that he cannot personally verify the health claims, says the plant grows outdoors in USDA zones 9 and up, and grows his in part shade near a pond. In cooler places, he suggests pots indoors by a window or under grow lights.

Indian doctors who have looked at viral claims land in the same place. In a January 2026 fact check by Medical Dialogues, Dr. G. Krishna Mohan Reddy, a diabetologist at Yashoda Hospitals, said the plant "cannot cure diabetes nor can it replace insulin or oral medications," and that using it without a doctor's guidance can cause dangerous low blood sugar.

What other health benefits have been studied?

Researchers have tested the plant for several other effects, almost always in rats, mice or lab dishes. The Hegde review lists these:

  • Cholesterol: Leaf extracts at 200 to 400 mg per kg reduced cholesterol, triglycerides and LDL in rats with high blood fats.
  • Antioxidant activity: Extracts showed antioxidant effects in lab tests, which fits the vitamins and flavonoids found in the leaves.
  • Antimicrobial activity: Extracts slowed the growth of bacteria such as E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae in the lab.
  • Kidney stones and urine flow: Some extracts acted as a diuretic in animals and changed how calcium oxalate crystals formed.
  • Cancer cells: Leaf and bark extracts slowed some cancer cell lines in lab dishes, which is a very early stage of research.

Some articles also claim liver and kidney protection. Those findings come from animal models of drug or diabetes damage, and none has been confirmed in people.

How do people use insulin plant leaves?

These are the traditional ways people use it. No research has set a safe daily amount, so this is description, not a dosing guide.

  • Fresh leaf: Washed and chewed raw, usually one leaf in the morning.
  • Leaf powder: Leaves are dried in the shade, ground, and taken by the teaspoon with water.
  • Tea: Fresh or dried leaves are steeped in hot water. This is common in the Philippines.
  • In food: Chopped into salads, smoothies or vegetable dishes, as some social media videos suggest.
  • Capsules and extracts: Sold online in India, the US and the UK, with strengths that vary from brand to brand.

If you have diabetes and want to try it, tell your doctor first and check your sugar more often than usual for the first few weeks.

Is the insulin plant safe?

For most people, eating an occasional leaf is unlikely to cause serious harm, but there are real risks for the people most likely to use it:

  • Low blood sugar: Combined with insulin, metformin, glimepiride or other diabetes medicines, it may push glucose too low. Watch for shaking, sweating, confusion and a fast heartbeat.
  • Mixed toxicity results: One rat study found no deaths at doses up to 5,000 mg per kg of an ethanol leaf extract. Another found signs of toxicity at 250 mg per kg of a methanol extract.
  • Stomach upset: Some people report nausea, loose stools or dizziness.
  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding: There is no safety data, so avoid medicinal amounts.
  • Children and pets: Keep supplements and powders out of reach.
  • Stopping your medicines: This is the biggest danger. Never cut or stop prescribed treatment because a plant seems to be working.

How do you grow the insulin plant at home?

It is an easy plant for Indian gardens and a good patio or indoor plant in colder places.

  • Light: Full sun to part shade. In hot Indian summers, afternoon shade keeps the leaves from scorching.
  • Soil: Fertile, moist soil that drains well. Mix in compost.
  • Water: Keep the soil evenly moist. Never let the pot sit in standing water.
  • Climate: Warm and humid. It is frost sensitive, so in the US it stays outdoors only in zone 9 and warmer, and in the UK it is an indoor or conservatory plant.
  • Propagation: Divide the clumps, root stem cuttings in water or soil, or replant the small plantlets that form under the flower heads.
  • Pests: Mites and nematodes can be a problem in light, sandy soil.

So, should you use the insulin plant?

As a garden plant, absolutely. It is pretty, tough and easy to share with neighbors. As a medicine, treat it as an unproven supplement. The animal results are interesting and a 2026 meta-analysis supports them, but the human evidence is one small study and a lot of personal stories. If you have diabetes, your medicines, food, activity and regular HbA1c tests do the real work. If you want to add the leaf on top, do it with your doctor in the loop and a glucose meter at hand.

This article is for general information only and is not medical advice.

FAQ

What is the insulin plant called in India?

Most people simply call it the insulin plant, in English or transliterated, such as "insulin ka paudha" in Hindi or "insulin chedi" in Tamil and Malayalam. In Siddha medicine it is known as kostum.

How many insulin plant leaves should I eat a day?

No study has set a safe or effective daily amount. Traditional use is one fresh leaf or one teaspoon of dried leaf powder a day, but that is custom, not evidence. Ask your doctor before starting.

Can the insulin plant replace insulin or metformin?

No. It contains no insulin, and no trial has shown it can replace any diabetes medicine. Stopping your prescribed treatment can lead to very high blood sugar and serious complications.

Can people without diabetes eat insulin plant leaves?

An occasional leaf is unlikely to harm a healthy adult, but there is no proven benefit for people with normal blood sugar. Skip it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.

How long does an insulin plant take to grow?

From a rooted cutting or rhizome, it grows quickly in warm weather and forms a leafy clump within a few months. It flowers in the warm season once established.

Is the insulin plant the same as crepe ginger?

No. Crepe ginger (Costus speciosus) is a taller relative with white flowers and red bracts. The two belong to the same plant family and are sometimes confused.
